Medes
mēdz
n. pl. (the people of Media, north-east of Babylon — the second horn of the ram, and the law that could not be altered)
From Hebrew Maday, Media or Mede — also the name of a son of Japheth (Gen 10:2), which places the nation in the Japhethite line. The Greek Medos follows.

Biblical Definition

The Medes occupied the highlands east of Assyria and north of Elam, and Scripture first mentions them as a place of exile: the ten tribes were settled “in the cities of the Medes” (2Ki 17:6). A century and more later Isaiah names them as the instrument of Babylon's fall, and adds a detail that no bribe would stop them: “Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it” (Isa 13:17). It happened. Daniel reads the writing on the wall and gives the interpretation: “PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians” (Dan 5:28), and that night the Chaldean king was slain. Thereafter Media and Persia are named together as one dual power, the ram with two horns, one higher than the other. Their most famous contribution to Scripture is constitutional: a signed royal decree was irrevocable, “the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” (Dan 6:8). Darius used it against himself and spent a sleepless night over a lions' den he could not open; Ahasuerus could not recall Haman's edict and had to issue a second. Medes are still present at Pentecost, listed among the nations that heard the wonderful works of God in their own tongue.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives Mede as a native of Media, an ancient country of Asia, and notes the joint empire of the Medes and Persians founded upon the fall of Babylon.

expand to see more

MEDE, n. A native or inhabitant of Media, a country of Asia lying south and west of the Caspian sea.

The Medes were descended from Madai, the son of Japheth.

In league with the Chaldeans they overthrew Nineveh, and afterward, with Cyrus, they took Babylon.

The laws of the Medes and Persians, once signed, might not be changed.

Darius the Median took the kingdom, being about threescore and two years old.

Key Scripture

Isa 13:17 — "Behold, I will stir up the Medes against them, which shall not regard silver; and as for gold, they shall not delight in it."

Dan 5:28 — "PERES; Thy kingdom is divided, and given to the Medes and Persians."

Dan 6:8 — "Now, O king, establish the decree, and sign the writing, that it be not changed, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not."

2Ki 17:6 — "In the ninth year of Hoshea the king of Assyria took Samaria, and carried Israel away into Assyria, and placed them in Halah and in Habor by the river of Gozan, and in the cities of the Medes."

Modern Corruption

An unalterable human law is admired as the height of legal order; Daniel and Esther both show it trapping the king who made it, and Scripture reserves immutability for God alone.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle worth recovering from the Medes is a doctrine of law. Their boast was a statute that could not be altered, and Scripture shows it twice producing absurdity: a king who loved Daniel obliged to throw him to lions, and an empire obliged to let a genocidal decree stand and merely arm its victims against it. Human law needs the power of repentance built into it, because human lawgivers are fallible and often malicious. What cannot change is God — “I am the LORD, I change not” (Mal 3:6) — and His immutability is safe precisely because His will is perfectly holy. Immutability in a fallen legislature is not majesty; it is a trap.

There is a second and happier thing here. The decree of Darius could not be altered, and neither could the covenant. The writer to the Hebrews reaches for exactly this legal picture: God, “willing more abundantly to shew unto the heirs of promise the immutability of his counsel, confirmed it by an oath” (Heb 6:17). What the Persian court could only counterfeit — a word that stands whatever comes — belongs in truth to the promise made to Abraham and sworn by God to Himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Maday (H4074), Madai, Media, Mede; Aramaic Maday (H4076); dath (H1881), a decree.

expand to see more

Hebrew Maday (H4074) — Madai; both the son of Japheth (Gen 10:2) and the nation sprung from him.

Aramaic Maday (H4076) — Mede; the form used in the Aramaic chapters of Daniel.

Aramaic dath (H1882) — decree, law; the unalterable statute of Dan 6:8.

Hebrew 'ur (H5782) — to stir up; the LORD's act in raising the Medes against Babylon (Isa 13:17).

Hebrew peras (H6537) — divided; the wall-word that announced the transfer of the kingdom.

Usage

"“Which shall not regard silver” — an army that could not be bought off."

"“Given to the Medes and Persians” — the sentence read off a plastered wall."

"“The law of the Medes and Persians, which altereth not” — a majesty that became a snare."
